newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee up for 3rd day, July leaps past $3.00.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee up for 3rd day, July leaps past $3.00.

text.p: The sizzling rally in CSCE coffee futures carried over to the third consecutive session Thursday, with benchmark July shattering the $3.00 a lb level as the broad-based buying frenzy continued, sources said.
July arabicas shot up to a life-of-contract high of 318.00 cents, the highest price in two decades, before closing at 314.80 cents, up 19.25 cents -- or more than six percent -- on the day.
Second-position September jumped 17.10 cents to 273.80 cents, while the back months rose 6.00 to 14.25.

"We are seeing history happen," said Christian Wolthers, vice president of Miami-based importer Blaser & Wolthers Specialty Coffee Trading Co. "We've not seen a market move like this without frost, drought or any other kind of tragedy. It is a clear situation of short supply for demand."

Consuming and producing countries' depleted inventories, which hover near 20-year lows, have been behind coffee futures sustained five-month run-up. Since the beginning of the year, the July contract has rallied more than 175 percent.

This week alone, the July contract has gained a whopping 57.95 cents -- or more than 22 percent. And market participants said the start of Brazil's winter is likely keep the market well underpinned over the next two months.
"In one week the (Brazil) frost season will be a baby and next month it's going to grow up," said Wolthers. "It is a dangerous situation with stocks in consuming countries so low."
Wolthers noted forecasts for a smaller 1997/98 crop in top-grower Brazil have also fueled the rally.

On Thursday, Brazil Specialty Coffee Association said it estimated the 1997/98 crop would reach 21.74 million 60-kg bags against 27 million bags in 1996/97. However, predictions for the coming Brazil crop have ranged widely between some 18 million and 27 million bags.

But as prices continue to march higher -- in the commodity pit and on the supermarket shelf -- some operators fear some consumers may balk at paying up and some roasters may jiggle their blends to include more lower-quality robusta beans.

"If New York sustains itself, you might see robustas rally even more," said Wolthers. "All beans roast brown, so it's the only escape roasters have. But a change in blends is another factor that can reduce consumption."
